Juvenile Painted rock lobsters (Panulirus versicolor) settling onto coral reef habitats undergo a dramatic metamorphic transition from their planktonic phyllosoma phase. Upon completing the final larval moult, the recently metamorphosed individuals emerge with a wet weight of approximately 0.01 grams , a mass that stands in stark contrast to the minuscule weight recorded at hatching. Detailed field studies of ovigerous females have revealed that individual eggs measure roughly one millimetre in diameter, and the resultant newly hatched larvae exhibit a wet weight measured at 0.000524 grams [Wwb = 0.000524 grams]. This figure represents the initial mass at birth and reflects the modest yolk reserves available to support the earliest free-swimming stages. Settlement occurs preferentially in shallow, structurally complex microhabitats where cover from predators is abundant. The ecological implications of this small initial mass are substantial, as it constrains the foraging window and necessitates rapid progression through successive moults.

Field surveys employing morphometric measurements across multiple populations have established an ultimate carapace length of 14.5 centimetres [Li = 14.5 centimetres] as the asymptotic size approached by the largest adults in undisturbed habitats. This value represents the mean maximum carapace length attained by older individuals under favourable environmental conditions, where competition for shelter and food resources is moderate. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight derived from the length-weight relationship for this species reaches approximately 1450 grams [Wwi = approximately 1450 grams] in fully grown adults, a body mass that positions Panulirus versicolor among the larger-bodied shallow-water spiny lobsters in the Indo-Pacific region. Sexual dimorphism in ultimate size is minimal, although gravid females often exhibit slightly broader abdomens to accommodate egg attachment. These asymptotic measurements were compiled from long-term mark-recapture programmes across the Great Barrier Reef and provide a robust baseline for evaluating growth performance against populations subject to varying fishing pressure.

Reproductive maturation in Panulirus versicolor occurs when females attain a carapace length at puberty of 8.2 centimetres [Lp = 8.2 centimetres], a threshold that typically corresponds to an age of several years under natural thermal regimes. At this developmental stage, gonadal activation commences and females become capable of mating and subsequently extruding fertilised eggs. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the maximum reproductive rate recorded for this species translates to an average of approximately 1290 eggs produced per day [Ri = approximately 1290 eggs produced per day], a value that integrates both the frequency of spawning events and the clutch size per event. This daily output is considerably higher than the rates observed in many temperate palinurid species and likely reflects an evolutionary adaptation to the high larval mortality typical of tropical pelagic environments. Individual clutches are carried by the female for several weeks until hatching.

The documented lifespan for Panulirus versicolor extends to approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years] when measured under the stable thermal conditions characteristic of mid-latitude reef environments at 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This longevity places the species among the longer-lived members of its genus, with individuals capable of surviving multiple decades if they avoid predation and fishing mortality. Age determination in this species is challenging owing to the absence of persistent calcified structures with clear growth bands; however, mark-recapture data combined with size-frequency analysis support a maximum longevity estimate of approximately three decades [am = approximately three decades]. Such an extended lifespan implies a relatively slow and continuous growth trajectory that continues long after the onset of reproductive maturity. Old individuals contribute disproportionately to the reproductive output of the population, as their larger body size allows them to produce larger clutches.

Comparative analyses of growth trajectories across the Indo-Pacific distribution of Panulirus versicolor suggest that the ultimate carapace length of 14.5 centimetres [Li = 14.5 centimetres] is attained only after many years of steady somatic expansion following each ecdysis event. Early benthic juveniles grow rapidly, adding mass at a rate that gradually decelerates as they approach the asymptotic size. The carapace length at puberty of 8.2 centimetres [Lp = 8.2 centimetres] represents a developmental milestone at which the energetic investment begins to shift from somatic growth toward gamete production. Notably, the wet weight recorded at the larval metamorphic transition is 0.01 grams , while the hatchling wet weight is 0.000524 grams [Wwb = 0.000524 grams], representing a roughly nineteen-fold increase in mass during the course of planktonic larval development. These early life-history parameters are critical inputs for demographic models assessing population resilience under varying climate scenarios.
